h1: How long homebrew keeps before it starts to fade
title: How Long Homebrew Keeps Before It Fades | Craft Beer School
desc: How long bottled and kegged homebrew stays fresh by style, the signs that it is fading and how storage changes the clock.
teaser: Some homebrew is best in a month. Some is better in a year. Here is how to tell which beer you have made.
standfirst: Homebrew does not go off like milk, but it does change. Hop aroma fades, malt flavours turn stale and some beers improve before they decline. How long yours keeps depends on the style, how it was packaged and where it is stored.
sections: Homebrew rarely goes unsafe, it goes stale

Beer made with clean kit and a healthy fermentation does not become dangerous with age. The alcohol, low pH, hop compounds and carbon dioxide make it a poor home for the microbes that cause food poisoning. What happens instead is a slow loss of quality. Fresh flavours fade and stale ones appear.

The main driver is oxygen picked up during packaging, working on malt and hop compounds over time. Heat speeds it up. Light can cause its own damage in clear or green glass. So the question is not whether old homebrew is safe to drink. It is whether it still tastes the way you wanted.

Hop aroma is the most fragile flavour in beer. The oils that give a pale ale or IPA its citrus, pine and tropical character are volatile and react easily with oxygen. Most hoppy homebrew is at its best within two to six weeks of carbonation. After two or three months even a well-made IPA will smell muted. The bitterness can turn harsh too.

That is why we tell students to brew hoppy beers in batches they will finish quickly. A 20 litre batch of IPA is 30 bottles of 650 ml. If that takes you four months to drink, brew 10 litres instead. Our guide to kegging homebrew explains why a cold keg holds hop aroma better than warm bottles.
A rough shelf life by style

• Hazy and West Coast IPAs, pale ales: best within one to two months, fresh as possible.
  • Wheat beers, Kolsch, light lagers, blondes: best within two to four months. Delicate malt and yeast character fades.
  • Bitters, amber ales, brown ales, everyday stouts: good for three to six months.
  • Belgian strong ales, barley wines, imperial stouts: often improve for several months and can keep for a year or more. Higher alcohol and darker malts resist staling and change in interesting ways.

These ranges assume cool, dark storage. Warm storage shortens every one of them.

Temperature matters most. A common brewing rule of thumb holds that staling roughly doubles in speed for every 10 °C rise. Beer kept at 4 °C in a fridge will taste fresh for far longer than the same beer in a cupboard at 30 °C. In much of India the cupboard is the bigger risk for most of the year. Our guide to first homebrew mistakes lists warm storage among the most common reasons good batches taste tired.

Light matters too. Brown bottles block most of the light that makes hoppy beer smell skunky. Green and clear bottles do not. Keep any bottle in a closed carton or a dark cupboard.
How to tell a beer is fading

Learn the signs and you will know when to drink up:

  • Muted aroma. A hoppy beer that once leapt out of the glass now smells faint or grassy.
  • Cardboard or wet paper. The classic stale note in pale beers.
  • Honey, toffee or sherry. Common in aged malty beers. Pleasant in a barley wine, unwanted in a lager.
  • Darker colour. Oxidised pale beers drift towards amber over time.

If the beer tastes sour, smells of vinegar or keeps getting more carbonated, the problem is infection, not age.
Tasting your own beer over time

The best way to learn how your beer ages is to taste it on purpose. Keep a few bottles of each batch back. Taste one at two weeks, one at two months and one at four months. Write a few words each time. You will learn which of your recipes hold up and which need drinking fast. It also trains your palate for the stale flavours above, which you will then notice in commercial beer that has sat in a hot warehouse too long.

Fermentation time matters too. A beer packaged before the yeast finished cleaning up can taste rough early and stale sooner. Our guide to how long beer takes to ferment covers that.

Your first step: label the next three bottles of your current batch with a date two weeks, two months and four months from today. Taste each on its date and write one line about what changed.
faqs: It rarely becomes unsafe, but it does go stale. Hop aroma fades and stale, papery or sherry-like flavours appear, faster in warm storage.
How long does bottled IPA last?
Hoppy beers are best within one to two months of carbonation. Keep them cold and drink them fresh.
Strong, dark and high alcohol styles such as barley wine, imperial stout and Belgian strong ales can improve for months.
